newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian central bank toughens its grip on banks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian central bank toughens its grip on banks.

text.p: Russia's central bank has improved and tightened its supervisory functions over commercial banks, but still has a long way to go in a sector haunted by fears of a new crisis, bankers say.

Banking analysts say only a fraction of Russia's 2,100 banks will survive, and the task of the central bank is to prevent major institutions from being affected or a systemic crisis from breaking out.

United City Bank banking analyst Andrei Yashchenko forecast that only a quarter of the current number of banks would survive over the next few months, but the shake-out would be a positive process leading to a healthier banking sector.
"This will not lead to mass bankruptcy but it may touch some of the larger banks, but not the biggest, as they have long ceased to operate with troubled banks," he said.
The central bank already shuts down dozens of smaller banks every month.

In recent months it has adopted a more active policy towards larger banks, taking them over when they get into difficulties, then restoring them to health if possible or stripping them of their licence.

On August 5 the central bank released Unikombank from its temporary administration but imposed temporary controls on medium-sized Kommerchesky Narodny Bank, the fourth Russian bank to be taken over in this way.

The imposition of temporary administration on major banks such as Unikombank, Russia's 12th biggest by assets and Tveruniversalbank, the 17th biggest, which lost its licence in July, fuelled fears of a crisis in the banking industry.

"The situation is quite difficult and it is only natural that the central bank is tightening its controls. It is keeping its hand on the pulse and trying to react quickly to changes," said central bank spokeswoman Natalya Khomenko.
Analysts said the central bank had toughened controls over banks in recent months by issuing new requirements for banks to be introduced gradually over the next two years.
The 12 requirements reflect recommendations of international organisations and the Association of Russian Banks.
For example, the minimum charter capital of a new bank was set at 2 million ecu ($2.53 million) on April 1, 1996, to be raised gradually to five million by July 1, 1998.
The central bank has transferred the supervision of major banks from its regional offices to headquarters, under a new system called OPERU-2, initially covering six of the biggest banks.
This will monitor credit lines, reserve levels, assets and liablities, in some cases on a daily basis.

"The central bank is advancing and is doing the right thing," Anatoly Milukov, deputy chairman at Mosbiznesbank, told Reuters. "But since such big banks have been in a crisis, it means it still lacks something."

In spring the central bank released AvtoVAZbank from its temporary administration and the bank said it made a 24.84 billion roubles ($4.68 million) pre-tax profit in the first quarter of this year after a 1995 loss of about 135 billion roubles.

Central bank management restructured the bank's balance sheet and made recommendations on the credit portfolio, and AvtoVAZbank closed several unprofitable branches, sold the premises and other real estate and halved its staff.
Analysts say many Russian banks face problems because of low capitalisation, risky credit policy and a stable rouble policy which has ended speculative profits from currency trading.
Government plans to drive down yields on the Treasury bill market will cut off another source of easy profits.
Alfa-Bank deputy chairman Pavel Gorbatsevich said the central bank had worked out a system of helping troubled banks and was spotting them much more quickly than before.
"During last August's (liquidity) crisis the central bank did not quite know what to do," he said. "Now it has worked out the approach of what to do with troubled banks."
Shareholders' funds at Unikombank grew 30 percent in two months when it was under central bank control.
But Gorbatsevich said the central bank was not quick enough in dealing with troubled banks.

"It introduces temporary administration only when rumours have been circulating on the market for some time that a bank has problems," he said. "But on the other hand as soon as the central bank starts paying particular attention to a certain bank, it ignites rumours." ($1=5305 Rouble) ($1=.7902 Ecu)
